blocks.content: Recall from the http-basics topic that every HTTP request carries a method, describing exactly what action the client actually wants performed. This topic covers the specific, standard methods in real, everyday use, and the genuinely important idea of idempotency, which of them are safe to retry without worry.

If you have ever seen GET or POST mentioned in a browser tool or an API document, this topic explains precisely what they mean, and why picking the right one actually matters, not just as a naming convention.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679021-390076409.png
1. GET: Retrieve a Resource

GET requests an existing resource, read only, with no intention of changing anything on the server at all. Loading a webpage, fetching a list of items from an API, checking a specific record, all of these are naturally GET requests.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679021-834215101.png
2. POST: Create or Submit

POST typically creates a new resource, or submits data for the server to process in some way. Submitting a form, creating a new user account, placing an order, these are all naturally POST requests, each one genuinely changing something on the server side.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679022-162273720.png
3. PUT and PATCH: Two Different Ways to Update
blocks.text: 3. PUT and PATCH: Two Different Ways to Update

blocks.content: PUT replaces an existing resource entirely, sending the FULL new version of it, whatever was not included is effectively considered gone. PATCH instead partially updates a resource, sending only the specific fields that actually changed, leaving everything else exactly as it was.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679022-752650408.png
blocks.alt: PUT and PATCH: Two Different Ways to Update

4. DELETE: Remove a Resource
DELETE, exactly as the name suggests, removes a resource. Deleting a post, removing an item from a cart, canceling an account, these are all naturally DELETE requests.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679022-213574871.png
5. Idempotency: A Genuinely Important Practical Concept
blocks.text: 5. Idempotency: A Genuinely Important Practical Concept

blocks.content: A method is idempotent if calling it multiple times in a row has the exact same effect as calling it just once. This matters enormously in practice, an idempotent request is genuinely safe to retry automatically, if a network hiccup makes you unsure whether the first attempt actually succeeded, sending it again causes no harm at all.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679022-462302506.png
blocks.alt: Idempotency: A Genuinely Important Practical Concept

blocks.title: Why this actually matters in real systems
blocks.content: Real networks are unreliable, exactly as the reliability-in-tcp topic covered. A client that is not sure whether a request actually succeeded needs to know whether simply resending it is safe, idempotency is precisely the property that answers that question.
6. Which Methods Are Idempotent

GET is idempotent, retrieving the same resource repeatedly never changes anything. PUT is idempotent too, replacing a resource with the exact same full new version repeatedly always ends in the exact same final state. DELETE is idempotent, deleting an already deleted resource again still just results in it being gone. POST is generally NOT idempotent, submitting the exact same form twice can genuinely create two separate new resources rather than one.

7. A Real World Example: A Typical API
blocks.text: 7. A Real World Example: A Typical API

blocks.content: A typical items API captures all of this together cleanly. GET /items lists every item. POST /items creates a brand new item. PUT /items/5 replaces item number 5 entirely with a new full version. DELETE /items/5 removes item number 5 completely. Each method name directly signals the client real intent before the server even looks at anything else in the request.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437679023-489676670.png
blocks.alt: A Real World Example: A Typical API

blocks.title: The same path, different methods, different meaning
blocks.content: Notice /items/5 means something different depending on the method used with it, PUT replaces it, DELETE removes it. The path identifies WHICH resource, the method identifies WHAT to do with it, they are two genuinely separate pieces of information.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Using GET for a request that actually changes something on the server, when GET is specifically meant to be safe, read only, and freely repeatable.","Assuming POST is safe to blindly retry after a network failure, when retrying it carelessly can genuinely create duplicate resources.","Confusing PUT, a full replacement, with PATCH, a partial update, they behave genuinely differently when fields are left out.","GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent and generally safe to retry; POST generally is not.","The right method choice directly communicates intent, both to the server and to anyone reading the API later."]
items: Using GET for a request that actually changes something on the server, when GET is specifically meant to be safe, read only, and freely repeatable.
Assuming POST is safe to blindly retry after a network failure, when retrying it carelessly can genuinely create duplicate resources.
Confusing PUT, a full replacement, with PATCH, a partial update, they behave genuinely differently when fields are left out.
GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent and generally safe to retry; POST generally is not.
The right method choice directly communicates intent, both to the server and to anyone reading the API later.
